before_text: Maintain a compatibility matrix for every route: exact model snapshot or negotiated protocol version; provider API, client SDK, and serving-runtime versions; lifecycle state and retirement date; supported request parameters and turn rules; tool protocol; JSON Schema support; context and output limits; refusal semantics; modality; processing geography and data policy; and tested quality slices. Managed agent runtimes and built-in tools belong in that matrix too. Record the agent runtime, tool versions, approval and sign-in behavior, state-retention rules, and retirement date. Then test the actual replacement before a preview or dated model shuts down. Treat aliases, defaults, and wrappers as mutable. Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, and AWS publish changes on different schedules, and platform-specific retirement dates can differ from a model creator's dates. Google's [Gemini deprecation schedule](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/deprecations) demonstrates why a product alias or managed surface needs its own migration owner even when the underlying model family remains available. A fallback that cannot honor the same contract puts the product in a different mode.

before_text: Calibrate a black-box judge on the exact endpoint, model version, rubric, language, and time window used for the release. Repeat representative judgments, record disagreement and rank stability, and require a human or deterministic fallback when the judge drifts. Do not transfer a calibration result across endpoints or silently updated aliases. A 52,988-attempt [study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04198) of shared judge endpoints found substantially lower repeat and next-day rank stability than a controlled endpoint. This makes local calibration an operating requirement rather than a one-time benchmark.

Probe an automated judge with controlled reversals. Hold the rubric fixed and change only the answer evidence that should affect the grade. Then hold the answer fixed and reverse a criterion whose judgment should change. A rubric-only baseline can reveal how much of the outcome is predictable without seeing the answer. Investigate that signal before trusting a high aggregate agreement score.

section: Section 8: Speculative decoding and runtime migration
before_text: When the rejection sampler and target-model sampling semantics are implemented correctly, speculative decoding preserves the target distribution. Use it to reduce latency, not to approximate an answer. Floating-point or batching nondeterminism still prevents any guarantee of byte-identical runs. Benchmark acceptance, draft and verification cost, TPOT, and SLO goodput at production concurrency. Low acceptance or saturated compute can make the system slower. [Leviathan et al.](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/leviathan23a.html) describe the method.
after_text:
When the rejection sampler and target-model sampling semantics are implemented correctly, speculative decoding preserves the target distribution. Use a verified lossless policy when preserving the target distribution is part of the contract. Floating-point or batching nondeterminism still prevents any guarantee of byte-identical runs. Benchmark acceptance, draft and verification cost, TPOT, and SLO goodput at production concurrency. Low acceptance or saturated compute can make the system slower. [Leviathan et al.](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/leviathan23a.html) describe the method.

Check the verification policy before treating speculative decoding as lossless. The vLLM v0.33.0 release notes at tag v0.33.0rc3 describe an opt-in lossy verifier and remove CUDA 12.9 release artifacts. Pin the serving image or wheel and verify its CUDA and framework requirements. Evaluate output quality separately before enabling any approximate verifier.
reason: Clarify that lossless speculative-decoding guidance does not cover an opt-in lossy verifier, and that serving-runtime upgrades require pinned CUDA/framework/artifact compatibility plus quality regression evidence. Accepted labels: REV-52. Primary URLs: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.33.0rc3.
consequence_accept: Readers can apply this bounded clarification with its primary evidence and limits.
consequence_reject: The current edition omits this verified operational clarification.
reader_what_changed: Separate lossless verification from opt-in lossy approximation and pin CUDA/framework/artifact compatibility.
reader_why: Clarify that lossless speculative-decoding guidance does not cover an opt-in lossy verifier, and that serving-runtime upgrades require pinned CUDA/framework/artifact compatibility plus quality regression evidence.

before_text: Monitor recalibration belongs in every model or reasoning-configuration migration. Compare action-only, reasoning-only, and combined monitoring where those signals are available and permitted. Measure detection, false alarms, and evasion on the same task slices. Treat those results as a reason to revalidate local monitoring, not as a production detection rate. Keep external receipts and enforceable policy checks independent of the monitor.

In predictive workflows, require every input feature to be available at the actual decision point. Use a paired test with a known leaking input and a valid control. Verify lineage and timestamps with a deterministic check. The clinical LeakBench preprint shows why an improved offline score can coexist with fatal prediction-time leakage.
reason: Add decision-time feature availability and provenance as evaluation invariants; a high offline score must not conceal a feature that cannot exist at the real decision point. Accepted labels: REV-54. Primary URLs: https://arxiv.org/html/2610.26088v1.
